opus-5.5.text:
I think the Computer-Using Agent idea is actually quite natural if you look at it from a reinforcement learning perspective. The core idea is that instead of building a special API or a custom integration for every single task, you let the model interact with the computer the same way a human does: it looks at the screen, it sees pixels, and then it outputs actions like moving the mouse, clicking, typing on the keyboard, scrolling. So the action space becomes very general. In principle, anything a human can do on a computer, the agent can also do.

That's why I think it's an important step. Before this, most "agents" were really function-calling systems. You give the language model a set of tools, it decides which tool to call, and the developer has to define everything in advance. That works well in narrow settings, but it doesn't scale to the long tail of real-world software, all these websites and desktop applications that have no clean API. The GUI is the universal interface. Humans designed all of these systems to be operated through a screen, so if you can master the screen, you get generality almost for free.

But of course, generality comes at a cost. When you operate at the level of clicks and keystrokes, the tasks become very long-horizon. Booking a flight might take dozens or even a hundred steps, and if you make a mistake in the middle, say you click the wrong date, the whole thing can fail. So the real challenge is not perception alone. Vision models are already pretty good at understanding screenshots. The challenge is reasoning and decision-making over many steps, recovering from errors, and knowing when to stop and ask the user for confirmation, especially for things like payments or logging in.

This is exactly where I believe reinforcement learning matters. You can't just do supervised learning on human demonstrations, because there's never going to be enough data covering every possible state, and the agent will inevitably drift into situations it has never seen. You need the model to actually try things in an environment, get feedback on whether it succeeded, and improve from that. I think what OpenAI did with Operator, combining GPT-4o's vision capability with reasoning trained through RL, points in that direction.

So my understanding is: CUA is less about a specific product and more about a paradigm shift. The agent is no longer a chatbot that tells you what to do. It's something that actually does the work for you inside the digital world. Right now it's still slow and makes mistakes, it's maybe at the stage of a fairly clumsy intern, but the direction is clear. Once the success rate on long tasks gets high enough, it will change how people use computers.

r001.rationale: The response describes screen-based actions, error recovery, and learning from environmental feedback, but does not clearly say that feedback from each action informs the model’s next action.

r002.rationale: It contrasts function-calling agents with GUI interaction, but does not explain that earlier frameworks supplied closed-loop behavior around foundation models that were themselves open-loop.

r003.rationale: It links Operator to vision capability and reasoning trained through RL, but does not attribute improved performance over traditional workflow agents to training specifically for computer interaction.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about Operator and the whole "Computer-Using Agent" idea is this: for the past couple of years, the industry has been building agents by giving models tools through APIs. You expose a function, the model decides to call it, you execute it. That works, but it only covers the tiny slice of the world where someone has written an API for you.

The CUA concept flips the premise. Instead of asking the world to adapt to the model, you let the model use the same interface humans already use: a screen, a mouse, a keyboard. It looks at pixels, decides where to click, types text, scrolls, and looks again. Once you can do that, the entire software ecosystem becomes your action space, including the long tail of websites and internal tools nobody will ever write an API for.

Technically, I see it as three pieces coming together. First, strong visual grounding: the model has to actually perceive a screenshot and localize things like buttons and form fields reliably, which turned out to be much harder than people expected. Second, long-horizon planning and recovery. A real task might take fifty steps, pages load slowly, popups appear, and the agent has to notice when something went wrong and backtrack rather than blindly continue. Third, and this is the part I think matters most, it was trained with reinforcement learning in real environments. Rather than imitating human click trajectories, the model is rewarded for completing the task end to end. That is what gives it the ability to improvise when the UI does not match its expectations.

What excites me as a researcher is that this makes the computer a general-purpose RL environment. Every website is a task, outcomes are often verifiable, and that is a very scalable source of training signal, in the same spirit as what we saw with reasoning models in math and code.

What I would temper expectations on is reliability. Benchmarks like OSWorld still show these agents far below human performance, latency is high, and there are real safety questions: an agent that can see the screen and click can also be manipulated by content on that screen through prompt injection. So I view Operator as a research preview that marks the direction, not a finished product. But the direction itself, I am quite confident about. In a few years, I think the question will not be whether a model can use a computer, but whether we still need humans to use most of them.

r001.rationale: It describes acting on the screen and then looking again, so the result of an action informs what the agent does next.

r002.rationale: It describes API-based agents, but does not explain that their foundation models are open-loop and that the framework supplies the closed-loop behavior.

r003.rationale: It says real-environment reinforcement learning helps the agent improvise, but does not clearly attribute better performance over traditional workflow agents to computer-interaction-specific training.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is that the computer becomes an interface an AI can use to carry out a task. A conventional chatbot tells you what to do; a computer-using agent can look at the screen, click buttons, type, and observe what changes.

That makes it a feedback loop: understand the goal, take an action, check the result, and decide what to do next. If you ask it to find a flight, for example, it needs to navigate the site, enter your requirements, and compare the options. It also needs to recognize when it lacks information or should ask you to confirm a consequential action.

So I would understand Operator through that broader concept: moving from generating answers to taking actions through a computer interface. The difficult part is making that process reliable—knowing whether an action worked, recovering when something unexpected happens, and staying within the authority the user has given it.

r001.rationale: It describes a feedback loop: take an action, check the result, and decide what to do next.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that earlier agent frameworks wrapped open-loop foundation models with closed-loop behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute improved performance over traditional workflow agents to training specifically for computer interaction.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that a Computer-Using Agent takes the interface we normally use—the screen, mouse, and keyboard—and makes it an action space for an AI agent. You give it a goal, and it looks at the screen, decides what to do, clicks or types, and then checks what happened. It keeps repeating that loop until it finishes or needs your help.

The important shift is from answering questions to carrying out tasks. If you ask an assistant to plan a trip, it can suggest flights and hotels. A computer-using agent could go through the websites and fill in the relevant information, with you confirming consequential actions such as a purchase.

What makes this interesting is that software doesn’t necessarily need a dedicated API for the agent to use it. The existing human interface becomes a broadly usable interface for AI. But that also creates the central challenge: interfaces are messy, actions can fail, and the agent has to recognize mistakes and recover. So I’d understand Operator as a step toward assistants that can act in digital environments, with reliability and human oversight being essential parts of that capability.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent checks what happened after clicking or typing and repeats the cycle, conveying that feedback informs later actions.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that earlier agent frameworks wrapped foundation models that were themselves open-loop.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute newer agents’ improvement over traditional workflow agents to training specifically for computer interaction.
